expectations.text: Explains the architecture taxonomy: A1 (full stack on premises), A2 (partial), A3 (connector), A4 (customer connector to external messaging), B (no local footprint — fully outsourced/browser access)
expectations.evidence: A1/A2/B roughly right but A3 described as Market Infrastructure connectivity and A4 as Lite2/bureau-hosted — wrong taxonomy (A3 is a connector on premises; A4 is a customer connector to external messaging).

expectations.text: States why it matters: architecture type drives which CSCF controls apply (mandatory/advisory/N-A per type)
expectations.evidence: 'Each architecture type maps to a specific applicable control set in the CSCF' — type drives applicable controls.

expectations.text: Notes the v2026 wrinkle: client connectors are mandatorily assessed under ~14 controls and some B users reclassify as A4
expectations.evidence: No v2026 client-connector ~14-control assessment or B-to-A4 reclassification.

expectations.text: Walks a determination method: inventory SWIFT-related components (messaging interface, communication interface, connectors, GUI) and where they run
expectations.evidence: Steps 1–3: map connectivity chain end to end, identify ownership/location of messaging interface, communication interface/SNL, HSM — inventory components and where they run.

expectations.text: Connects to attestation: the type selected in KYC-SA determines the control set attested against — misclassification is an assessment finding
expectations.evidence: 'Your KYC-SA attestation submission requires you to declare your architecture type. Declaring the wrong type is itself a compliance/accuracy problem'.
